What’s buzzin’, cousin?
wuts BUZ-in KUZ-in
phrase (Silent Generation slang)
A rhyming jive greeting, current in the 1940s and still heard among 1950s teenagers; it was popular enough to give its title to a 1943 Hollywood musical. Buzz is imitative, the hum of bees; it also came to mean a low murmur of talk or a rumour, and the greeting asks, in effect, "What’s the talk? What’s new?" Cousin here is not kin; it is chosen for the rhyme and the friendliness.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

"What’s buzzin’, cousin?" was the bright, rhyming hello of the jive era — a sailor on leave in 1944, a soda jerk in 1951, anyone who wanted to sound hep. It meant "How are you? What’s new?" and the person greeted was no more a cousin than the moon. Scripture is full of greetings, and they are better than ours. Boaz walked into his barley field and said to the reapers, "The LORD be with you. And they answered him, The LORD bless thee" (Rut 2:4). The risen Christ came to frightened disciples behind shut doors and said, "Peace be unto you" (Joh 20:19). Paul closed his letters with greetings by name. A greeting is a small act of love; it tells a person he is seen. The question in the jive phrase is also worth answering well. The buzz of the world is mostly rumour, and Christians are told to starve it: "where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth" (Pro 26:20). But there is news worth passing on: "As cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country" (Pro 25:25). And the best answer to "What’s buzzin’?" is the oldest good news there is: "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings" (Isa 52:7) — Christ is risen, and He saves sinners.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (a rhyming jive greeting of the 1940s–50s) for What’s new? How are you? — from the 1828 buzz, a whisper or report spread secretly, and an invitation to pass on good news rather than rumour (Pro 25:25).

WHAT’S BUZZIN’, COUSIN?, phr. (Silent Generation slang, 1940s–50s; jive) A rhyming greeting: What’s new? How are you? "Hey, Eddie — what’s buzzin’, cousin?"

Webster (1828) — BUZZ, verb intransitive 1. To make a low hissing sound, as bees; to make the sound of z, with an expiration of breath between the tongue and the roof of the mouth or upper teeth. 2. To whisper; to speak with a low hissing voice; to make a low hissing sound. BUZZ, verb transitive To whisper; to spread, as report, by whispers, or to spread secretly. BUZZ, noun The noise of bees; also, a whisper.

Decode for families: it is just "hi, what’s new?" — the cousin is only there for the rhyme.

Key Scripture

Rut 2:4 — "And, behold, Boaz came from Bethlehem, and said unto the reapers, The LORD be with you. And they answered him, The LORD bless thee."

Joh 20:19 — "Then the same day at evening, being the first day of the week, when the doors were shut where the disciples were assembled for fear of the Jews, came Jesus and stood in the midst, and saith unto them, Peace be unto you."

Pro 26:20 — "Where no wood is, there the fire goeth out: so where there is no talebearer, the strife ceaseth."

Pro 25:25 — "As cold waters to a thirsty soul, so is good news from a far country."

Isa 52:7 — "How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good, that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!"

Modern Corruption

A cheerful, harmless greeting; the only caution is that "the buzz" can mean gossip, and a Christian should pass on good news, not rumour.

expand to see more

There is nothing wrong in this greeting. It is friendly, silly, and musical, and it made people smile. Rhyming hellos like it (see you later, alligator) were the play of a generation that had come through a depression and a war and wanted to laugh.

The one thing to watch is in the word buzz itself. A buzz is a murmur passing from ear to ear, and the buzz is often gossip. When a friend asks what’s buzzing, a Christian can decline to pass along the rumour (Pro 26:20) and find something better to share — a kindness, a prayer answered, the good tidings of the gospel.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Imitative buzz (the hum of bees) → a murmur, a rumour → 1940s jive greeting "What’s buzzin’, cousin?" → 1950s teen hello.
